name: Enzyme Activity Calculator
seoDesc: Enzyme activity is the rate at which a preparation converts substrate, expressed in units. Free enzyme activity calculator: enter your values and get substrat
summary:
Enzyme activity is the rate at which a preparation converts substrate, expressed in units. It returns substrate converted, activity and specific activity, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator converts between absorbance change per minute, units per mL and units per mg, using the extinction coefficient of the product and the light path. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Enzyme Activity
sections.html:
Activity (µmol/min) = (ΔA/min ÷ (ε × l)) × volume; 1 U = 1 µmol/min

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
ΔA/mininitial rate from the linear part of the curveAU/min
εextinction coefficient of the absorbing speciesM⁻¹cm⁻¹
lpath lengthcm
volumetotal reaction volumemL

Where the relationship comes from. IUBMB enzyme unit definition; ε₃₄₀ for NADH = 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹.

sections.title: How do I use the Enzyme Activity?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: absorbance change per minute of 0.05 AU/min, molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, path length of 1 cm, reaction volume of 1 mL, protein in the assay of 0.1 mg.

Substituting them into the formula gives substrate converted of 0.008 µmol/min, activity of 8,038.59 U/mL, specific activity of 80.39 U/mg.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
linear phaseUse thisthe first 10–20% of substrate conversion
plateauDo not usesubstrate depletion or product inhibition
lagDo not usetemperature equilibration

  • Only the initial linear rate is a measure of activity. Once the curve bends, you are measuring the assay, not the enzyme.

  • NADH and NADPH absorb at 340 nm with ε = 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, which is why so many coupled assays are read at that wavelength.

  • Units must be quoted with temperature, pH and substrate concentration, or they are not comparable.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Using the extinction coefficient of NAD⁺ instead of NADH (NAD⁺ barely absorbs at 340 nm).
  • Reading a plate without correcting for path length, which is much shorter than 1 cm.
  • Fitting the whole curve rather than the linear portion.

faq.a: One micromole of substrate converted per minute under the stated conditions.

faq.q: Why does my rate fall off?
faq.a: Substrate depletion, product inhibition, or enzyme instability. Measure earlier in the curve.

faq.q: What does the Enzyme Activity actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns substrate converted, activity and specific activity. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
